newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Tobacco deal, Marsh Mac and GE.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Tobacco deal, Marsh Mac and GE.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

So far so good on the tobacco front for insurers. Reuters insurance journalists have contacted a range of underwriters from around the world and the feeling seems to be the $368.5 billion settlement agreed on Friday will not hit them to any great extent.

Insurers were not directly included in the deal, and Louisiana is expected to drop 120 insurance companies from its lawsuit. Some insurers feel this proves that insurers are protected by tobacco exclusionary clauses and other strong wordings, and on the whole feel pretty pleased with themselves.
Cigarette manufacturers could perhaps turn to policies written before the U.S. Surgeon General's report on smoking in the early 1960's, but it appears unlikely.

The situation is not yet finalised. Vice-President Al Gore this morning said parts of the deal might have to be rewritten, and there is still the possibility of class actions against cigarette retailers. Many Americans feel there should be a stronger element of "punishment" in the settlement, and by that they mean more money. If the funds of manufacturers are sealed shut, they may well look for other ones to open.
--oo0oo--

There is a suggestion in the market that General Electric is considering buying U.S. broker Marsh & McLennan. Or at least that seems to be the suggestion - a British newspaper on Sunday suggested that in fact it was the other way round and that Marsh would buy GE.

Marsh is locked in battle with Aon for supremacy in the global insurance sector, and between them they have bought up a huge chunk of the other major businesses, to the extent that options for growth may be exhausted.
The suggestion is that by teaming up with GE, Marsh would ensure its position as the biggest insurance broker in the world.
A leading Marsh executive joked at a meeting in London on Monday that he was only in town to sell lightbulbs, but there are reasons why a merger might work.

GE Capital, the financial services sided of GE, has been spending up to $10 billion a year on acquisitions, many of them in the insurance sector. Its biggest insurance acquisition so far was Employers Re which has assets of more than $20 billion and which itself acquired Frankona Re and Aachen Re in Germany.
Some brokers at Lloyd's argue that tie-ups by brokers with large industrial or financial conglomerates are inevitable as they seek to compete with each other and expand their businesses.

Others feel it is the smaller firms that will grow. Marsh and Aon have been hit by major staff defections, which could lose them business if clients move their accounts to the departing teams' new companies. Last week Tony McCallum, chairman of Carpenter Bowring, part of Marsh's operations in London, left the group to join the smaller London-based broker Jardine Lloyd Thompson. This follows the departures of 15 senior brokers at Aon's London-based Bain Hogg, who joined the British-based interests of Arthur J. Gallagher, a large US broker and a major rival of Aon and Marsh.
It may not be long before we have a new big six.
--OO0OO--
